The flow envisioned with this approach works like this:
The application loads an NFT with the default localization as defined by the creator.
User would then interact with the NFT within the application to translate fields to a localized version if one is provided and so desired.
If the user interacts to translate, via dropdown or if set in a global application setting (i.e. translate to "dn" if available) :
3a. Make a secondary request to pull localized data and modify the original object on the application side with the localized data.

The rationale here is that if there are localization options for the NFT then the application will still have to make a second request regardless to pull the requested localized data which can then just be used to alter the localized fields. A few localization options would result in a just a few KB but, at scale repeating the data 155 times for all possible localization options would be a huge waste if repeating the entire file.
Perhaps an even better improvement would be to add all localization options to a singular file like this:
https://metadata.xr-art.com/nft/000B013A95F14B0E44F78A264E41/localizedFields.json

This approach would allow for many localizations to be handled in the same file which significantly increases scalability, decreases storage requirements and minimizes the number of files that need to be tracked.

A disadvantage to this approach would be an increased probability of application error for deeply nested localized fields. One way to mitigate this risk would be to provide localization directly in the original metadata but, could result in bloated and useless data.

since XLS20 seems to be only 2 weeks away from implementation onto main net I want to stoke conversation on this again.

XLS24 gives a lot of flexibility for future use cases beyond just art, but the immediate implications and use case in the next few months will be 95% art based NFTs. Thinking in broader terms of not just on the XRPL, but across the whole industry, projects should be cognizant of implementing a minimum standards (similar to the opensea standard) of sorts for easy implementation and compatibility. Many of the large EVM based chains have very similar metadata standards with small deviations/differences.
The Base Art NFT example above seems to fill that minimum standard.

A thought on adding collection attributes. on EVM chains collections are mutable user defined within marketplaces. NFTs are grouped based on the contract they were minted from, but users can add new NFTs from other sources into a collection. There are both pros and cons to adding collection attributes into the metadata itself.

The metadata file should have both IPFS CIDv1 and CIDv0 like this image.

IPFS gives you for the NFT the CIDv0 but then what appears in the explorers is CIDv1. So there is always uncertainty about the true correspondence between the CIDv0 and the corresponding CIDv1. It exists the tool (CID inspector) that converts one to the other, but that information should be in the metadata file in order to anyone check the correspondence directly just opening the metadata file, not having to go to the CID inspector to make sure there is correspondence.
(To check in Bithomp: https://bithomp.com/explorer/rMGqQpJnjZhd64uzGzq7Zm1AZG7iD7NTu1
